https://artdaily.com/news/198808/Poland-.text: Home Last Week Artists Architects Galleries Museums Photographers Photography PhotoGallery Games Subscribe Comments Search Contact Poland Pavilion at Gwangju Biennale 2026 presents Rites of Passage Inside Job (Ula Lucińska and Michał Knychaus). Photo: Weronika Pawlak / Adam Mickiewicz Institute. GWANGJU .- What happens when one chapter of life has come to an end, but the next has yet to begin? Rites of Passage, an exhibition organised by the Adam Mickiewicz Institute for the Poland Pavilion at Gwangju Biennale 2026, explores the experience of transition—both on a personal and a global scale. The exhibition is curated by Paulina Olszewska and brings together artists from Poland and Korea: Alicja Bielawska, Urszula Broll, Inside Job (Ula Lucińska and Michał Knychaus), Park Saengkwang, Yeesookyung, and Anna Zaradny. Rites of Passage will be presented as part of the 16th Gwangju Biennale, held this year under the theme You Must Change Your Life. One of the most important contemporary art events in Asia, the Biennale will run from September 5 to November 15, 2026. We live in a time of constant flux, yet we increasingly lack shared rituals that help us navigate through it. What was once embedded in the rhythm of communal life—transitions between life stages, mourning, coming of age, the beginning of a new chapter—has often become a private experience, difficult to articulate. It is precisely this condition that Rites of Passage seeks to explore. The exhibition takes as its starting point a passage from The White Book, written by Han Kang during her stay in Warsaw in 2016. In it, the author reflects on a moment of hesitation: the threshold between what has already happened and what is yet to come. It is a moment of uncertainty, anticipation, and stepping into the unknown. For curator Paulina Olszewska, this image became the starting point for a broader reflection on rites of passage—those moments when our lives change, sometimes dramatically, sometimes almost imperceptibly. From birth to death, from personal decisions to historical turning points, change is a constant presence. It shapes our everyday lives, memory, relationships, and communities. The rite of passage is not merely the subject of the exhibition—it is also embedded in its spatial design. Visitors will move through a sequence of environments, ranging from spaces of subtle, almost imperceptible transformation to areas defined by distinct thresholds, tensions, and ruptures. In one section, the artworks will gently merge into one another, suggesting change as a gradual process. In another, visitors will encounter contrast, dissonance, and a sense of disruption. The journey through the pavilion becomes a physical experience of crossing a threshold—of moving from one state of being to another. The exhibition also responds to the theme of the 16th Gwangju Biennale, You Must Change Your Life. In a world marked by war, the climate crisis, social tensions, and increasing polarisation, transformation is no abstract concept. It is something we experience every day—in our private lives, in politics, in society, and in our relationships with others. The exhibition brings together different generations, artistic traditions, and media. Traditional painting and drawing meet installation, video, sound, ceramics, textiles, and objects made from both organic and industrial materials. Works by Alicja Bielawska, Inside Job, and Anna Zaradny are presented in dialogue with historical works by Urszula Broll and Park Saengkwang—widely regarded as one of the leading figures of modern Korean art, whose work has become an enduring part of Korea’s cultural heritage—as well as an installation by Yeesookyung. Together, they create a multisensory environment in which materials, images, sounds, and textures evoke an atmosphere of contemplation, suspension, and transformation. A specially commissioned sound composition will form an integral part of the exhibition. Rooted in the traditional music of the region while incorporating experimental approaches to sound, it will serve as an acoustic guide through the exhibition—a sonic landscape accompanying visitors as they move through the successive spaces of the pavilion. Rites of Passage has been conceived as an open exhibition, without providing a single prescribed narrative or any straightforward answers. Each visitor is invited to experience it in their own way, interpreting its symbols, tensions, and transitions through the lens of their own sensibility. It is a space for contemplation: intimate and personal, yet deeply attentive to the contemporary world. Viewed through both Polish and Korean perspectives, the exhibition becomes a shared meditation on change—inevitable, unsettling, yet profoundly human. The Poland Pavilion at Gwangju Biennale is organised by the Adam Mickiewicz Institute with support from the Embassy of the Republic of Poland in Seoul, the ING Polish Art Foundation, Galeria Studio and leeleenam studio. Project is funded by the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage of the Republic of Poland. The Adam Mickiewicz Institute (IAM) brings Polish culture to people around the world. Being a state institution, it creates lasting interest in Polish culture and art through strengthening the presence of Polish artists on the global stage. It initiates innovative projects, supports international cooperation and cultural exchanges. It promotes the work of both established and promising artists, showing the diversity and richness of our culture. The Adam Mickiewicz Institute is also responsible for the Culture.pl website, which is a comprehensive source of knowledge about Polish culture. https://www.andoveradvertiser.co.uk/news.text: Scouting Clubs and societies Leisure Andover Oliver Webster selected to deliver World Scout Jamboree By Sophie Day Reporter Share 0 Comments Oliver Webster has been selected to help deliver the World Scout Jamboree in Poland in 2027. (Image: Supplied) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. An Andover Scout has been selected to help deliver the World Scout Jamboree in Poland in 2027. Oliver Webster will join a UK team of 600 volunteers who will play a key role in delivering the international event, which brings together young people from nearly every country around the globe. Oliver will collaborate with Scouts worldwide to help create a once-in-a-lifetime experience for young people aged 14 to 17. Read more Scouts from Hampshire prepare for global jamboree Volunteers needed to help launch new Girls' Brigade group in town PICTURES: Lawn tennis club marks 90th anniversary with new courts Dozens of young people honoured for achieving highest DofE award End of an era as 1st Andover Girls’ Brigade bows out after 99 years Oliver Webster has been selected to help deliver the World Scout Jamboree in Poland in 2027. (Image: Supplied) He said: "I am honoured to have been selected for the International Service Team at the World Scout Jamboree. "This is a unique opportunity to support an event that brings together young people from around the world, and I look forward to helping create an unforgettable experience for all participants." The World Scout Jamboree is held every four years and offers young people the chance to explore different cultures, build friendships and develop skills for life. In 2027, more than 50,000 Scouts will gather in Gdansk, Poland, to celebrate international friendship, adventure and global citizenship. Chief Scout Dwayne Fields congratulated Oliver and the other volunteers chosen for the event. He said: "Congratulations to Oliver and all the UK volunteers heading to the World Scout Jamboree in Poland. "Opportunities like this are what Scouting is all about, bringing people together, building confidence, and showing young people what’s possible when they step outside their comfort zone. "The Jamboree is more than an event, it’s a chance to connect with the world, to learn from different cultures, and to come back inspired to make a difference at home. "I’ve no doubt they will grab this experience with both hands and make the most of every moment." As part of an International Team, Oliver will be involved in running outdoor activities, supporting cultural exchanges or helping to deliver large-scale events that celebrate global diversity. His role will contribute to the smooth running of the Jamboree and ensure a meaningful experience for all who attend. The 26th World Scout Jamboree promises to be a major gathering of young people united by the spirit of Scouting. http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27929.text: Big News Network.com EU urges Kiev to mobilize women - Moscow Brussels believes the move is needed to address the Ukrainian military's severe manpower shortage, according to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service Brussels is encouraging Kiev to start mobilizing women amid chronic manpower shortages and has demanded that Ukraine immediately make "a political decision" on the matter, the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) has said. Kiev launched its mobilization campaign soon after the conflict with Russia escalated in February 2022. Amid mounting frontline losses and desertions, the mobilization drive has grown increasingly violent. Recruitment officers have repeatedly been filmed chasing, beating, and forcibly detaining reluctant conscripts before bundling them into vehicles in what in Ukraine has become known as "basification." EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, described the idea of expanding the campaign to include women as "a step in the right direction" at a recent informal EU foreign ministers' meeting, the SVR said on Thursday, citing information it had obtained. She allegedly warned that Kiev could soon run out of manpower due to a growing shortage of men fit for military service and said that Ukraine should use Israel as a "model to follow." The mobilization of women has long been a subject of debate in Ukraine. MP Mariana Bezuglaya argued as early as 2024 that it was time Kiev started targeting women to meet its conscription quota. Last year, the Ukrainian presidential administration's deputy head, Brigadier General Pavel Palisa, also voiced support for mandatory conscription of women. According to the SVR, Brussels demanded that Kiev immediately "move from words to action" and make a formal decision to start mobilizing women. Under current Ukrainian law, men aged 25 to 60 are subject to mobilization, while those aged 23 to 60 are generally barred from leaving the country. Women can serve voluntarily. Kiev's brutal mobilization campaign has encountered large-scale draft-dodging and desertion. According to Euronews, around 1.15 million fighting-age Ukrainian men had ended up in the EU as of summer 2026, despite the ban on travelling abroad. According to the SVR, up to 5.6 million Ukrainians are currently residing in various European nations, with women accounting for 43.4% of them. Many men have proven ready to risk their lives to flee the country illegally through forests, rivers, and mountainous terrain. In February, the head of the Ukrainian border agency, Andrey Demchenko, reported that over 70 apparent draft dodgers had died since 2022, most while trying to cross the Tisza River along Ukraine's border with Hungary and Romania. Brussels has reportedly urged EU governments to devise legal mechanisms for sending back Ukrainian refugees residing in the bloc, the Russian intelligence service said, adding that the European Commission sees them as a reason behind the "rise of far-right sentiment" in countries such as Germany or Poland. Some Western officials have also voiced support for the mobilization of Ukrainian women. Last year, former British Defense Secretary Ben Wallace said that Vladimir Zelensky should have launched a truly mass mobilization and conscripted all men and women, without sparing the younger generation. "Zelensky took a view that he was going to preserve the 18 to 28-year-olds, so it's not a mass conscription," Wallace said at the time, adding that the Ukrainian leader should have mobilized everyone and "asked Europe to train them because that is not a hard ask." Ben Hodges, a former top commander of US forces in Europe, argued earlier that Kiev should consider both drafting women and lowering the mobilization age to 18. "I also think that there is enough work for women in the army," he stated. Moscow has repeatedly slammed Ukraine's NATO backers as pushing the nation into a war "to the last Ukrainian," describing the conflict as a Western proxy war against Russia fought through Ukraine. Skip next section Kolkata police issues prohibitory order after stampede 10/18/2026 October 18, 2026 Kolkata police issues prohibitory order after stampede 25 people were injured in the crush, some of whom are in critical condition Image: AFP Authorities in the city of Kolkata have imposed restrictions in the area around Chor Bagan after a stampede at a Durga Puja pandal killed at least 19 people. The order prohibits gatherings of five people or more, processions, public meetings, slogans or public speeches. It will remain in place until October 20. Similar instructions were imposed in central Delhi and other cities during protests led by India's Cockroach movement. In a notification announcing the order, Kolkata police said it had received intelligence warning of a possible law and order problem, news agency ANI reported. Earlier on Sunday, the city's police formally arrested seven people in connection with the stampede at the Chorbagan Sarbojonin Durgotsab Samity Durga Puja pandal. As per Indian media, at least 19 people have died due to the crush on Saturday evening and several others remain in critical condition. https://p.dw.com/p/5ONXA Skip next section Truck hits devotees in Gwalior, kills at least 13 10/18/2026 October 18, 2026 Truck hits devotees in Gwalior, kills at least 13 The truck reportedly sped through police barricades before losing control Image: ANI/Handout/REUTERS At least 13 people were killed and 40 others injured on Sunday morning in India's central city of Gwalior, authorities said, after an out-of-control truck hit a crowd of devotees. Indian media reported that the truck, loaded with paddy, broke through police barricades before it lost control and crashed into a temple's outer wall and gate. The incident occurred around 1:30 a.m. local time Sunday (2000 GMT Saturday). Gwalior Senior Superintendent of Police told News agency ANI that the incident occurred in an area where heavy vehicles are restricted. Of the injured, five to six people were in a critical condition. An eyewitness told ANI that they saw some people die on the spot. "The truck was overloaded; it came suddenly and ran over some shops and people. My brother also sustained injuries," the witness said. Others complained of delayed assistance and confused Information on treatment. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he was "distressed" to learn about the "mishap," announcing monetary compensation for the next of kin to each of those who lost their lives. "I express my deepest condolences to the bereaved families and pray for the swift recovery of those injured," Indian President Droupadi Murmu said on social media. India, with 1.4 billion people, recorded more than 183,000 road traffic deaths in 2025, or over 500 a day, according to the roads ministry. The temple in question was devoted to an Indian Goddess, Sheetla Mata, who is revered for her healing powers and her association with relief from fever and disease. Her devotees conduct certain ceremonies in the early hours of the morning when temperatures are cool. Her worship typically focuses on practices such as cold food offerings and avoiding use of fire. https://p.dw.com/p/5ONFf Skip next section Kolkata stampede: Police detain 12, chief minister vows strict action 10/18/2026 October 18, 2026 Kolkata stampede: Police detain 12, chief minister vows strict action Relatives of the stampede's victims described confusion and darkness inside the venue before the incident Image: AFP Police in India's eastern metropolitan city of Kolkata detained 12 people on Saturday night, including the organizers of Chor Bagan Durga Puja, as they probe a stampede that killed nearly 20 people. The latest update from the state's Chief Minister's X account puts the death toll at 17, with another 25 injured. However, Indian media, including news agency Press Trust of India (PTI), reported that at least 19 people had died. The detentions came after West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari promised strict action against those who failed to carry out their duties to maintain crowd safety. "We have detained 12 people in connection with our probe into the Chor Bagan incident. Our officers are talking to them to find out the cause that led to today's mishap. If any lapses are found, we will act as per the law," the officer told PTI. Meanwhile, the West Bengal government has announced an independent investigation into the matter, led by a sitting judge of the city's high court. "We will check the footage and take appropriate measures against those who failed to manage the crowd. That could be a member of the puja committee, a homeguard, a temporary worker, a policeman, or a private company security guard. Nobody will be spared," Adhikari said. The politics of Durga Puja Stampedes at religious and cultural festivals are not uncommon in India, but Adhikari's government is under pressure to make the city's biggest annual festival a hit this year. Adhikari belongs to Prime Minister Narendra Modi 's right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party which won the state elections in West Bengal for the first time in India's history, ending former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee's 15-year rule there. The festive season was facing pressure even before it began. Food and fuel inflation , worsened by the conflict in the Middle East and lower than normal rainfall at home, is eating into people's disposable incomes. Amit Shah, India's Union Home Minister — and Modi's right-hand man — is set to visit the victims and their family members on Sunday morning. The minister had arrived in Kolkata on Saturday evening for a series of festive programs which have now been postponed. Dharvi isn't the only one stepping away from her desk as India kicked off its festive season last week. We're currently in the middle of Navratri and Durga Puja, festivals celebrating the different forms of the Indian Goddess Durga. Kolkata's Durga Puja pandals are known for their grandeur and high artistic expression Image: Dibyangshu Sarkar/AFP Navratri — which translates roughly to 'nine nights' — is fervently celebrated across north and western India with colorful dances and vegetarian delicacies. In the east, Durga Puja takes on an artistic fervor, where numerous beautiful tents are set up to welcome the Goddess back to her maternal home. They herald the countdown to India's biggest festival of the year, Diwali. But the festive cheer has been dampened, at least temporarily, in the eastern state of West Bengal. On Saturday evening, heavy crowds, rain and inadequate safety measures led to a stampede in the city fo Kolkata, killing over a dozen people and injuring several more. Stay tuned for updates on that and more from India on Sunday. https://p.dw.com/p/5ONBX Skip next section Many killed in stampede at religious festival in Kolkata 10/17/2026 October 17, 2026 Many killed in stampede at religious festival in Kolkata Dmytro Hubenko A pandal is a temporary structure that houses idols of the goddess Durga [FILE: October 16, 2026] Image: Dibyangshu Sarkar/AFP At least 17 people, including 13 women and a child, were killed in a stampede at the Durga Puja religious festival in North Kolkata that was likely caused by sudden rainfall. "Today (17/10/26), at around 19:40 hrs, a stampede occurred at the exit gate of the Sarada Park (Chor Bagan) Puja Pandal in the Girish Park Police Station area due to heavy crowds of pandal visitors amid rain," the Kolkata Police said in a statement, adding that the injured were taken to the hospital. West Bengal's Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari told reporters that the fatalities included a seven-year-old girl and that 25 others were injured in a stampede. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi called the incident "extremely distressing" and announced interim compensation for the families of those who died. The largest annual Hindu festival in India's eastern state of West Bengal, Durga Puja attracts thousands of devotees to temporary structures called pandals that house idols of the goddess Durga. Poor management and safety lapses at large events in India, such as religious festivals, often result in deadly crowd incidents. The movement published a photo of him on X in which it referred to Dipke as "a free man." The CJP's head of legal affairs, Ratna Singh, said Dipke was released after agreeing to certain conditions. She did not provide details about the terms. Neha Bora, a prominent student activist and the face of the protests, was also detained on Friday while attempting to reach central Delhi with dozens of supporters. Indians in Berlin are joining calls for accountability over controversial voter list revisions. https://p.dw.com/p/5OMFv Skip next section Supreme Court says access to internet fundamental right for children, calls blanket bans 'disproportionate' 10/17/2026 October 17, 2026 Supreme Court says access to internet fundamental right for children, calls blanket bans 'disproportionate' India's top court declared that access to and use of the internet is a fundamental right of every individual, including children, legal news outlet LiveLaw reported Saturday. It said that a blanket ban on children's internet activity could make them vulnerable to greater risks rather than protect them from online abuse and exploitation . The Supreme Court also issued directions to bolster the processes for detecting and removing child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) from social media and other online platforms, the report said. The court stressed that the right to freedom of speech and expression also incorporates the right to know, receive and impart information and ideas, LiveLaw reported. The two-judge bench described the internet as a "marketplace of ideas, creative expression and information" and said that its value went beyond the material it contains, as it provides opportunities for children in remote areas and those with disabilities. "For many children, particularly in remote areas, it is often the only source of learning and information," the court said, according to LiveLaw . For children with special needs, the internet is often the only platform where they can find company with others like them, the court said. The court acknowledged that the internet, in its current form, poses safety risks to children. But it said that keeping children away from the internet because of failures by platforms and the relevant authorities to detect and remove harmful content would amount to mistaking the victim for the problem, LiveLaw reported. What did the court say on blanket restrictions on internet use for children? The Supreme Court said that a legal ban would not stop children from using the internet, and that they could move to other unregulated platforms. "Any blanket restriction on the access of internet by children is nothing more than unproven measures of proven disproportionality," LiveLaw cited the court as saying. The Supreme Court called for safeguards to ensure online child safety and the regulation of content accessible to children. It suggested measures such as a "child mode" for social media accounts, LiveLaw said. Saturday's Supreme Court judgement comes amid a global debate on the ban of social media for children over risks from harmful content. Australia declared the world's first social media ban for under-16s last year. France followed suit this summer, before its Constitutional Court blocked the move . The US representatives include Pramila Jayapal, Ilhan Omar, Jim McGovern, Rashida Tlaib, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Jesus Garcia. "As the world's largest democracies, the US and India have an obligation to promote and defend the rights to freedom of assembly and expression," Jayapal wrote on X, sharing a letter addressed to Rubio. The letter alleges a "pattern of repression, wrongful detention, and excessive use of force by security forces" during the student protests in Delhi and other parts of the country. The lawmakers also highlight incidents of "apparent surveillance," saying that they had received reports that the Indian diplomatic missions in the US "hired photographers to surveil protesters on American soil." "These incidents raise particular alarm in light of India's documented pattern of engaging in transnational repression, including through the weaponization of consular services, harassment, intimidation, and physical violence," the letter said. The group urged Rubio to prioritize the issues in his discussion with Indian officials. The US Secretary of State is visiting India early next week, after traveling to Uzbekistan. He is slated to meet Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar in Mumbai. His agenda also shows a trip to Jamnagar in the western state of Gujarat.
